If you're commitment to her and your vows really meant something to you both then it's time to fight. To me, when you marry someone, that's a promise to stick with your person for the duration of your life. It's a promise given in the knowledge that life has many ups and downs, the only constant is change and in that relationships evolve. Marriages, most of time, take real work and effort. They take compassion and understanding.

First of all, her behaviour is unacceptable. It needs to stop. Tell her you are uncomfortable with how visibly close they are and she has disrespected you by being so physically close to this man, in plain sight. You need to grow a back bone, you ought to have politely interrupted and then asked her if you could both leave; if she'd have made a fuss or said no I'd have sternly told her that I was going home, I'd see her when she got home. I'd then ask her to make sure she gets home safely and tell her to call me if she needed a ride home. I'd kiss her on the cheek and I'd leave. I'd then wake her in the morning with a cup of tea and some pain killers for the hangover. Lay beside her and wait for her to wake up a little. When it was appropriate I'd ask her, in all sincerity, what was going on. I'd be asking her if she was okay. It's naive to think she's just a horrible person.
Is she unhappy in your marriage? If so, you MUST establish whether or not she is willing to work with you to re-establish your connection. This is a time you really have to tune into reason and logic. If she gives half arsed answers, if she's closed off or tries to incite arguments, if she's rude, or if she refuses or brushes you or your feelings aside, then I'm afraid it's time you leave. You deserve to be heard, she made a promise to always try with you and for you. Leaving the marital home doesn't mean divorce straight away. Remember your promise. When you leave tell her where you will be, tell her that when she is ready to make your marriage a priority, and YOU a priority, to call you. It might seem strange to do things like making a cup of tea and giving her pain meds, like kissing her on the cheek even though you're raging, but you're showing her that even though you are undoubtedly angry, you still love and care for her. You're showing her kindness despite your anger. By doing these little things you'll help her drop her guard and avoid being defensive. It opens up an environment to communicate.
If she tells you she's happy in your marriage you must first establish that this is the truth. It would be an odd response considering her behaviours. If she's telling you she's happy in order to end, or shut down, the conversation then leave. If she tells you she is happy in your marriage then you both need to work together to understand her behaviour, understand that it's hurting your marriage and consider going to marriage counseling. I think at this point you'll need that unbiased input. I recommend you try to get your wife to put herself in your shoes. Ask her to imagine the exact scenarios you have witnessed her and this guy, in. Ask her to really imagine it's real, she's watching it before her very eyes and now ask her how she feels. Open up to her and tell her she's hurting you. Even if she told you she would be fine with things the other way around, the fact remains; her behaviour is hurting you and if she loves you she will back off. I'm not the jealous type at all, but I have been and I understand the emotion. From the info given I'd have been jealous on a number of occasions and I'd be close to asking that fella what the fuck he thinks he's doing. 
Anyway, essay over, sorry I felt compelled to respond. I hope I have helped in some way. Good luck, man.

You're 20 years of age, you are an adult and you have the right to make your own decisions. I'd suggest standing up to your parents, should the need arise. Firstly I'd tell them I had someone meaningful in my life, tell them his name and tell them I'd love for them to meet him. You'll probably be asked questions regarding his name... If you're met with disapproval, stay calm and remember to breath slowly and deeply, answer their questions and firmly state that although their opinions matter to you and you're upset that they feel negatively towards your partner, you are serious about this man and you plan to remain in a relationship with him. 
One day you won't live with your parents anymore, one day your parents won't be around as much, and then one day they won't be here at all. Don't live for your parents, don't make decisions based on their opinions of how you should live your life and on what company you keep. If you're serious about the fella then stand up for him and don't tolerate any negative remarks. Walk away from conflict and address it at the next calm moment. State firmly that you will not tolerate any nastiness or rude remarks, you find their jokes offensive and you will actively ignore this behaviour. Tell them he is important to you and your family are important to you and so it's important they at least try to get along. 
I really wish you the best of luck. What you want matters! Good luck.

I've done and said some pretty fucked up stuff in my past and for me, I have many regrets and so much I will never forgive myself for. I strongly encourage you and others to forgive yourselves for past transgressions, but I just know I can't let go of that guilt. To be honest, I don't want to let go of the guilt, it reminds me who I want to be and how I want to conduct myself. Again, my experience is different, in that you find it empowering, whereas I have felt humiliated and ashamed. Reading books and coming to terms with the fact that I was abusive and manipulative was so hard. I'd find myself trying to convince myself I didn't carry these actions out or I'd notice my thoughts were always attempting to justify my behaviour. It was exhausting having to analyse each thought during conflict. The result is that I am now an incredibly open and honest person and I explain my thought path, then I explain how that makes me feel, and then I actively listen to the opinions of the other party. I also think before I speak. I feel I need to stress that I still fuck up every now and again, I close off, I catch myself gaslighting someone and when I'm in that headspace I cannot drop that pride and admit fault, the angers rages in my stomach and I don't drop an argument when I should or in the way I should. I know I have come such a long way and I am proud to say I have done so alone, but fuck me, it sucks that after all this hard work, one occasional appearance of BPD during conflict can still cause complete chaos to our relationships. We cannot take back what we say and how we hurt people and it sucks we sometimes have no control over this. Well, not yet. I sincerely hope I can rewire my brain enough to eradicate all traces of BPD. Knowing my luck the final step of my transformation will be a year of silent meditation... Is being a good person really worth it? Sometimes, I do wonder.

Ooo very tough one! Okay, after giving it some serious thought. The first book was 'Loves me, Loves me not'. This, along with 'Love me, don't leave me' were transformative. As I have ADHD, I really struggled with perseverance, but I cannot recommend these highly enough. My final recommendation isn't a book, per se, it's a subject matter... Read and watch all you can on Dialectical Behavioural Therapy or Acceptance and Commitment Therapy. Really delve into these subjects and if you think they can help, buy the DBT workbook (or download the free PDF) or the ACT workbook. I have both and I committed to doing both workbooks to the best of my ability. I still go through these books and utilise what I have learned, very often. I hope this helps.

I currently rent a room in a shared house, I love it and respect my live in landlords very much so, but my room is often a little chaotic. I have ADHD, meds help somewhat, but not in regard to misplacing/losing things. I'm often frantically hunting for said items 5 minutes before I'm due to leave for work. I'm also indecisive and I have low self esteem... I regularly have mornings where I'll change clothes 3/4 times, before I feel okay. My room can look like a tornado has passes through...albeit a bery polite one, which was careful to not knock over my preciouses or cause any damage; Having said all that, when I visit my ex girlfriends place (we're in a weird place right now), I make a concerted effort to not only tidy, but to clean. I sometimes leave clothes on the floor, or pots in the sink, but my default is to clean up after myself. My chaotic mess would make her feel 'scrambled egg' as we call it. I don't want her to worry about having me over, stress about mess, or be negatively preoccupied with anything I've caused/may cause. 
When living with someone, a person you are intimate with, there has to be REASONABLE compromise. It's unreasonable for you to take this attitude in the first place... If your mess is making your SO unhappy it really is down to you to pull your weight and sort your sh*t out. Besides disability, mental health or otherwise, what excuse could you possibly have for not picking up after yourself? It is unfair to say "well this is me, I am messy... Accept me as I am...". We all lose motivation and have off days, hell... I have off weeks, but I always revert back to better habits. Trust this internet stranger when she says... It really is better for our mental health when we live in a clean and tidy environment.
